section: 1. Base de dados e fundamentos
title: PhysioBank, PhysioToolkit, and PhysioNet: Components of a New Research Resource for Complex Physiologic Signals
authors: Ary L. Goldberger, Luís A. N. Amaral, Leon Glass, Jeffrey M. Hausdorff, Plamen Ch. Ivanov, Roger G. Mark, Joseph E. Mietus, George B. Moody, Chung-Kang Peng, H. Eugene Stanley
abstract: PhysioNet (http://www.physionet.org) is a new resource for biomedical research and education funded by the National Institutes of Health. PhysioNet offers free access via the Internet to large collections of recorded physiologic signals (PhysioBank) and related open-source software (PhysioToolkit). The overall goal is to stimulate current research and new investigations in the study of complex biomedical and physiologic signals.
raw_citation: GOLDBERGER, A. L. et al. PhysioBank, PhysioToolkit, and PhysioNet: components of a new research resource for complex physiologic signals. Circulation, v. 101, n. 23, p. e215–e220, 2000. DOI: 10.1161/01.cir.101.23.e215.

section: 1. Base de dados e fundamentos
title: MIMIC-III, a Freely Accessible Critical Care Database
authors: Alistair E. W. Johnson, Tom J. Pollard, Lu Shen, Li-wei H. Lehman, Mengling Feng, Mohammad Ghassemi, Benjamin Moody, Peter Szolovits, Leo Anthony Celi, Roger G. Mark
abstract: MIMIC-III ('Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care') is a large, single-center database comprising information relating to patients admitted to critical care units at a large tertiary care hospital. Data includes vital signs, medications, laboratory measurements, observations and notes charted by care providers, fluid balance, procedure codes, diagnostic codes, imaging reports, hospital length of stay, survival data, and more. The database supports a wide range of analytical applications spanning epidemiology, clinical decision-rule improvement, and electronic surveillance techniques.
raw_citation: JOHNSON, A. E. W. et al. MIMIC-III, a freely accessible critical care database. Scientific Data, v. 3, n. 1, art. 160035, 2016. DOI: 10.1038/sdata.2016.35.

section: 1. Base de dados e fundamentos
title: MIMIC-IV, a Freely Accessible Electronic Health Record Dataset
authors: Alistair E. W. Johnson, Lucas Bulgarelli, Lu Shen, Alvin Gayles, Ayad Shammout, Steven Horng, Tom J. Pollard, Sicheng Hao, Benjamin Moody, Brian Gow, Li-wei H. Lehman, Leo Anthony Celi, Roger G. Mark
abstract: The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV is a contemporary electronic health record dataset covering hospital admissions to Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between 2008 and 2019. MIMIC-IV incorporates a modular structure that separates in-hospital emergency department and ICU data, improves patient tracking across hospitalizations, provides out-of-hospital mortality link, and standardizes data elements to enable broad machine learning and clinical discovery.
raw_citation: JOHNSON, A. E. W. et al. MIMIC-IV, a freely accessible electronic health record dataset. Scientific Data, v. 10, n. 1, p. 1, 2023. DOI: 10.1038/s41597-022-01899-x.

section: 1. Base de dados e fundamentos
title: MIMIC-IV-Note: Deidentified Free-Text Clinical Notes (Version 2.2)
authors: Alistair Johnson, Tom Pollard, Steven Horng, Leo Anthony Celi, Roger Mark
abstract: MIMIC-IV-Note provides deidentified free-text clinical notes for patients admitted to the hospital and intensive care units at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. The dataset includes discharge summaries and radiology reports containing detailed clinical narratives, diagnostic impressions, patient histories, hospital course descriptions, and recommendations, forming the premier public benchmark for clinical NLP and LLM evaluation.
raw_citation: JOHNSON, A.; POLLARD, T.; HORNG, S.; CELI, L. A.; MARK, R. MIMIC-IV-Note: deidentified free-text clinical notes (version 2.2). PhysioNet, 2023. DOI: 10.13026/1n74-ne17. Disponível em: https://physionet.org/content/mimic-iv-note/2.2/. Acesso em: 29 out. 2026.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Potential of GPT-4 for Detecting Errors in Radiology Reports: Implications for Reporting Accuracy
abstract: To investigate the potential of GPT-4 for detecting errors in radiology reports and assessing reporting accuracy. GPT-4 was evaluated on simulated and clinical radiology reports containing intentional typographical, lateralization, and anatomical discrepancies. The model achieved high sensitivity in detecting errors, demonstrating substantial promise as an automated proofreading assistant to reduce diagnostic discrepancies.
raw_citation: GERTZ, R. J. et al. Potential of GPT-4 for detecting errors in radiology reports: implications for reporting accuracy. Radiology, v. 311, n. 1, e232714, 2024. DOI: 10.1148/radiol.232714.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Large-Scale Validation of the Feasibility of GPT-4 as a Proofreading Tool for Head CT Reports
abstract: A large-scale multicenter study validating GPT-4 as an automated proofreader for emergency and inpatient head computed tomography (CT) reports. The study evaluated thousands of reports to measure accuracy in detecting lateralization mismatch (e.g., left vs right hemisphere), numerical and measurement inconsistencies, and omission of critical diagnostic findings.
raw_citation: KIM, S. et al. Large-scale validation of the feasibility of GPT-4 as a proofreading tool for head CT reports. Radiology, v. 314, n. 1, e240701, 2025. DOI: 10.1148/radiol.240701.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Improving Radiology Report Error Detection Using a Multipass Large Language Model: Framework Development and Validation
abstract: Standard single-prompt LLM error detection can miss subtle contextual errors in complex medical reports. This study develops a multipass large language model framework dividing report checking into distinct verification stages (lexical, anatomical, clinical consistency, and impression alignment), demonstrating significant improvements in sensitivity and specificity over baseline models.
raw_citation: KIM, S. et al. Improving radiology report error detection using a multipass large language model: framework development and validation. JMIR Medical Informatics, v. 14, e87368, 2026. DOI: 10.2196/87368.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Large Language Models for Error Detection in Radiology Reports: A Comparative Analysis Between Closed-Source and Privacy-Compliant Open-Source Models
abstract: To address patient privacy and institutional compliance when using generative AI, this paper conducts a direct head-to-head comparison between cloud-based closed-source models (such as GPT-4) and on-premises privacy-compliant open-source models (such as LLaMA and Mistral variants) in identifying diagnostic, anatomical, and transcript errors in radiology reports.
raw_citation: SALAM, B. et al. Large language models for error detection in radiology reports: a comparative analysis between closed-source and privacy-compliant open-source models. European Radiology, v. 35, p. 4549–4557, 2025. DOI: 10.1007/s00330-024-11005-5.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Generative Large Language Models for Detection of Speech Recognition Errors in Radiology Reports
venue: Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, v. 6, n. 2, e230205
abstract: Speech recognition technology is ubiquitous in clinical radiology dictation but frequently introduces homophone substitutions, dropped negation words (e.g., 'no pneumothorax' transcribed as 'pneumothorax'), and punctuation slips. This study evaluates how well generative LLMs identify and rectify speech recognition errors in clinical radiology documentation.
raw_citation: SCHMIDT, R. A. et al. Generative large language models for detection of speech recognition errors in radiology reports. Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, v. 6, n. 2, e230205, 2024. DOI: 10.1148/ryai.230205.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Generative Large Language Models Trained for Detecting Errors in Radiology Reports
abstract: Investigating domain-adapted generative LLMs fine-tuned specifically on synthetic and real clinical radiology corpora with annotated reporting errors. The trained models demonstrate superior calibration, reduced false-positive flags, and nuanced understanding of medical imaging terminology compared to general-purpose LLMs.
raw_citation: SUN, C. et al. Generative large language models trained for detecting errors in radiology reports. Radiology, v. 315, n. 2, e242575, 2025. DOI: 10.1148/radiol.242575.

title: Large Language Model–Assisted Radiology Report Quality Assurance: Real-World Multicenter Evaluation
venue: Journal of Medical Internet Research, v. 28, e106250
abstract: A multicenter prospective evaluation of an automated LLM quality assurance pipeline integrated into active radiological workflows. The authors analyze detection of side discrepancies, critical incidental findings, recommendation tracking, and radiologist acceptance rates in routine clinical hospital care.
raw_citation: WANG, L. et al. Large language model–assisted radiology report quality assurance: real-world multicenter evaluation. Journal of Medical Internet Research, v. 28, e106250, 2026. DOI: 10.2196/106250.

section: 2. LLMs para detecção de erros, avaliação e qualidade em textos médicos
title: Systematic Evaluation of the Quality of Synthetic Clinical Notes Rephrased by LLMs at Million-Note Scale
authors: Jinghui Liu, Sarvesh Soni, Anthony Nguyen
abstract: Large language models can synthesize clinical text for applications ranging from documentation assistance to privacy-preserving data augmentation. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of LLM-generated clinical text covering intrinsic linguistic quality, extrinsic predictive utility, and factuality across one million synthetic clinical notes rephrased from the MIMIC database.

venue: Journal of Medical Internet Research, v. 28, e94689
abstract: Clinical validation of multilingual and Chinese-adapted large language models for identifying semantic discrepancies, anatomical mismatch, and typographic errors in non-English radiological documentation. The findings highlight cross-lingual transfer capabilities and domain-specific calibration requirements.
raw_citation: ZHOU, J. et al. Error detection and correction in Chinese radiology reports using large language models: real-world clinical validation study. Journal of Medical Internet Research, v. 28, e94689, 2026. DOI: 10.2196/94689.

title: A Dataset and Benchmark for Hospital Course Summarization with Adapted Large Language Models
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, v. 32, n. 3, p. 470–479
abstract: Hospital course summarization requires synthesizing long, heterogeneous inpatient EHR documentation into a coherent summary. This work releases a multi-hospital clinical benchmark and evaluates instruction-tuned and domain-adapted LLMs, assessing clinical accuracy, temporal coherence, and hallucination rates.

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently hallucinate findings in chest X-ray and CT interpretation. This work introduces Clinical Contrastive Decoding (CCD), a training-free inference-time intervention that contrastively suppresses visual language hallucinations.
